title: Maximum and minimum on a closed interval
objectives: Prove that a continuous function on a closed interval attains its maximum and minimum.

screens.title: Four functions with no top
screens.prose: None of these four functions attains a largest value. Flip through them. Each breaks one of three conditions: a closed interval, a bounded interval, a continuous $f$.

state.caption: A: $f(x) = \tfrac1x$ on $(0, 1]$. It climbs without bound near 0.

frames.caption: A: $f(x) = \tfrac1x$ on $(0, 1]$. It climbs without bound near 0.
B: $f(x) = x$ on $[0, 1)$. It creeps towards 1 but never gets there.
C: $f(x) = x$ on $[0, 1)$ and $f(1) = 0$, on $[0, 1]$. The top is missed again.
D: $f(x) = x$ on $[0, \infty)$. It rises for ever.

screens.question: Match each picture to the condition it breaks.

hints.text: Look at each end of each interval. Is it included?
A misses 0 and B misses 1. C includes 1 but jumps there.
D runs on for ever. Differentiability is not one of the three conditions.

feedback.correct: Right. Open ends in A and B, a jump in C, no end in D.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each picture ask: is each end included, is there an end, and does the graph jump?

byKey.t5: Differentiability is not needed. $|x|$ on $[-1, 1]$ has a corner and still attains its maximum 1.
byKey.t3: Only C jumps. A, B and D are continuous where they are defined.
byKey.t4: Only D has no right end. A and B live inside $[0, 1]$.

explain.text: A and B lose their top at a missing end point. C includes the end, but the jump at 1 drops the value to 0. D has no end, so it rises for ever.

canvas.caption: C: $f(x) = x$ on $[0, 1)$ and $f(1) = 0$, on $[0, 1]$. The top is missed again.

screens.title: A function that has a top
screens.prose: Now $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$ on $[0, 2]$: continuous, on a closed bounded interval. Its extremes can only be at the end points or where $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 0$, that is $x = 1$.

state.caption: Each dot rises or falls to the value you type.

screens.question: Fill in $f$ at the three candidates.

hints.text: The values are $0$, $-2$ and $2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute each $x$ into $x^3 - 3x$.

explain.text: The largest value is 2, at the end point $x = 2$. The smallest is $-2$, at $x = 1$, where the tangent is flat. Both are attained, as the hook's four functions were not.

screens.title: A top reached twice
screens.prose: Widen to $[-2, 2]$. Now $f'(x) = 0$ at $x = -1$ and $x = 1$, and the end points are $-2$ and 2.
screens.question: Select all that apply: where is the maximum attained?

options.why: You picked a flat point. $f(1) = -2$ is the minimum.
$f(-2) = -8 + 6 = -2$, the minimum again.
$f(0) = 0$. It is neither the top nor the bottom.

hints.text: Work out $f$ at all four candidates.
Both give 2, the largest value.

feedback.correct: Right. The maximum 2 is attained at $x = -1$ and at $x = 2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Evaluate $f$ at $-2$, $-1$, 1 and 2 and pick every place where the largest value occurs.

explain.text: $f(-1) = f(2) = 2$ and $f(1) = f(-2) = -2$. So the maximum is attained twice, once inside and once at an end. The theorem promises a maximum, not a unique place.

screens.title: The extreme value theorem
screens.prose: **Extreme value theorem.** If $f$ is continuous on a closed bounded interval $[a, b]$, then there are $c, d \in [a, b]$ with $$f(c) \le f(x) \le f(d) \quad \text{for every } x \in [a, b].$$ We prove it in two parts: $f$ is bounded, then its sup is attained.
screens.question: Which of these does the theorem guarantee for a continuous $f$ on $[a, b]$?

options.text: A largest value $f(d)$, attained at some $d \in [a, b]$.
A point where $f' = 0$.
options.why: You mixed in Rolle. The theorem needs no derivative, and $f(x) = x$ on $[0, 1]$ has no flat point.

options.text: The largest value sits at an end point.
options.why: You generalised from $[0, 2]$. On $[-2, 2]$ the top is also reached inside, at $x = -1$.

options.text: The largest value is attained at exactly one point.
options.why: You added uniqueness. On $[-2, 2]$ the top 2 is reached twice.

hints.text: The theorem talks about values of $f$, not slopes.
Look back at $[-2, 2]$: where was the top?
It promises existence of a top value, nothing about where or how often.

feedback.correct: Right. A top value exists and is attained.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate what the theorem says from what our examples happened to show.

explain.text: Continuity plus a closed bounded interval give a maximum and a minimum that are attained. Where they sit and how often is not promised. Each of the hook's pictures broke one hypothesis.

screens.title: Part 1: suppose it is unbounded
screens.prose: Part 1 proves $f$ is bounded, by contradiction. Suppose no $M$ has $|f(x)| \le M$ for all $x \in [a, b]$.
screens.question: What does that let us pick?

options.text: For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, a point $x_n \in [a, b]$ with $|f(x_n)| > n$.
The points $x_n = a + \tfrac{b - a}{n}$.
options.why: You picked fixed points. Nothing says $f$ is large at them; unboundedness only says some point beats each $n$.

options.text: One point $x$ with $|f(x)| = \infty$.
options.why: You gave $f$ an infinite value. Every value is a real number; unbounded means no single bound works.

options.text: Points $x_n$ with $|f(x_n)| > M$ for one fixed $M$.
options.why: You fixed the bound. To build a contradiction we need values beyond every $n$, so the bound must grow.

hints.text: Negate 'there is $M$ with $|f(x)| \le M$ for all $x$'.
Negation: for every $M$ there is $x$ with $|f(x)| > M$.
Use $M = n$ for each $n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate the statement '$f$ is bounded', then take $M = 1, 2, 3, \dots$

explain.text: Not bounded means every $M$ fails: some $x$ has $|f(x)| > M$. Taking $M = n$ gives a sequence $x_n$ with $|f(x_n)| > n$. The sequence lives in $[a, b]$.

screens.title: A subsequence that settles
screens.prose: The points $x_n$ all lie in $[a, b]$, but they may jump about.
screens.question: What gives a convergent subsequence $x_{n_k} \to c$?

options.text: Bolzano-Weierstrass (l9): $(x_n)$ is bounded.
Monotone convergence: $(x_n)$ is increasing.
options.why: You assumed an order. Nothing makes $x_n$ increase; they come from wherever $f$ is large.

options.text: No subsequence is needed: $x_n \to c$.
options.why: You let the whole sequence converge. It may jump between two places; only a subsequence is promised.

options.text: $(x_n)$ is Cauchy, since its terms lie in $[a, b]$.
options.why: You took bounded for Cauchy. $0, 1, 0, 1, \dots$ lies in $[0, 1]$ and is not Cauchy.

hints.text: What do we know about $(x_n)$? Only that it is bounded.
Which level-2 theorem starts from a bounded sequence?
Every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.

feedback.correct: Right. Bounded, so a subsequence converges.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the only fact we have: $a \le x_n \le b$.

explain.text: $(x_n)$ is bounded by $a$ and $b$, so Bolzano-Weierstrass gives $x_{n_k} \to c$. Nothing more is known about the order of the $x_n$. That is why l9 is the engine of this proof.

screens.title: The limit stays inside
screens.prose: The limit $c$ must be a point where $f$ is defined, or continuity cannot be used. On $(0, 1]$ that fails: $\tfrac1n \to 0$.

state.caption: $x_n = \tfrac1n$ in $(0, 1]$ tends to 0, which is outside.

screens.question: Why is $c \in [a, b]$?

options.text: $a \le x_{n_k} \le b$ for every $k$, and limits keep $\le$, so $a \le c \le b$.
Each $x_{n_k}$ is in $[a, b]$, and so the limit is too, for any interval.
options.why: You trusted any interval. On $(0, 1]$ the points $\tfrac1n$ tend to 0, outside it; closedness is what helps.

options.text: Because $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$.
options.why: You used continuity to place $c$. Continuity at $c$ needs $c$ in the domain first.

options.text: Bolzano-Weierstrass puts the limit in the interval.
options.why: You asked too much of l9. It gives a limit; where the limit lies depends on the ends.

hints.text: Each term satisfies $a \le x_{n_k} \le b$.
Limits preserve non-strict inequalities.
So $a \le \lim x_{n_k} \le b$; strict ends would fail.

feedback.correct: Right. Closed ends survive the limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pass the inequalities $a \le x_{n_k} \le b$ to the limit.

explain.text: From $a \le x_{n_k} \le b$ we get $a \le c \le b$. With an open end, as on $(0, 1]$, the limit can escape. This is where 'closed' enters the proof.

screens.title: Part 1 assembled
screens.prose: Prove that a continuous $f$ on $[a, b]$ is bounded. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $f$ is unbounded. For each $n$ pick $x_n \in [a, b]$ with $|f(x_n)| > n$.
$(x_n)$ is bounded, so by Bolzano-Weierstrass a subsequence $x_{n_k} \to c$.
Since $a \le x_{n_k} \le b$, the limit $c$ lies in $[a, b]$.
$f$ is continuous at $c$, so $f(x_{n_k}) \to f(c)$; a convergent sequence is bounded.
But $|f(x_{n_k})| > n_k \ge k$, so $(f(x_{n_k}))$ is unbounded. Contradiction. $\blacksquare$
By continuity, $f(x_n) \to f(c)$ for the whole sequence.
lines.why: Only the subsequence converges to $c$. The whole $(x_n)$ may not converge at all.

lines.text: Each $x_n$ is in $(a, b)$, so $c \in (a, b)$.
lines.why: The limit can be an end point. Closedness gives $c \in [a, b]$, which is all we need.

hints.text: Start with the contradiction hypothesis and the points $x_n$.
Then a subsequence, its limit in the interval, and continuity there.
Finish by comparing bounded with unbounded.

feedback.correct: Right. Pick, extract, stay inside, then continuity clashes with $|f| > n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The order is: pick points, extract a subsequence, place its limit, use continuity, contradict.

byKey.d1: You used the whole sequence. Only the subsequence is known to converge.
byKey.d2: You placed $c$ strictly inside. It may be $a$ or $b$; continuity on $[a, b]$ covers those too.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Three hypotheses each do one job. Bounded gives Bolzano-Weierstrass, closed keeps $c$ in the interval, and continuity at $c$ makes $f(x_{n_k})$ converge. A convergent sequence cannot exceed every $k$.

screens.title: Part 2: the top is reached
screens.prose: Now prove the supremum is attained. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: By part 1, $f$ is bounded, so $M = \sup\{f(x) : x \in [a, b]\}$ exists by completeness.
For each $n$, $M - \tfrac1n$ is not an upper bound, so pick $x_n$ with $f(x_n) > M - \tfrac1n$.
By Bolzano-Weierstrass and closedness, a subsequence $x_{n_k} \to d \in [a, b]$.
$M - \tfrac{1}{n_k} < f(x_{n_k}) \le M$, so $f(x_{n_k}) \to M$ by the squeeze. By continuity, $f(x_{n_k}) \to f(d)$.
Limits are unique, so $f(d) = M$: the maximum is attained at $d$. $\blacksquare$
Since $M$ is the supremum, pick $d$ with $f(d) = M$.
lines.why: You assumed the sup is a value. That is what we are proving; for $x$ on $[0, 1)$ it is not.

hints.text: Name $M$ first, then points whose values approach it.
$M - \tfrac1n$ fails to be an upper bound, which supplies $x_n$.
Then subsequence, squeeze, continuity, uniqueness of limits.

feedback.correct: Right. Approach the sup, extract, and let continuity hand over the value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build $x_n$ with $f(x_n) \to M$, extract a subsequence, then use continuity.

byKey.d1: You took the sup as attained. On $[0, 1)$, $\sup x = 1$ is never a value; closedness is needed.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: The squeeze sends $f(x_{n_k})$ to $M$ and continuity sends it to $f(d)$. One sequence has one limit, so $f(d) = M$. The minimum follows by applying this to $-f$.

screens.title: Where the slope is zero
screens.prose: A classmate finds the maximum of $x^3 - 3x$ on $[0, 2]$ by solving $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 0$. They get $x = 1$ and say the maximum is $f(1)$.
screens.question: Is the classmate right?

options.text: No. $f(1) = -2$ is the minimum; the maximum 2 is at the end point $x = 2$.
Yes: the maximum is always where $f' = 0$.
options.why: You checked only flat points. On a closed interval the end points are candidates too, and here $f(2) = 2$ wins.

options.text: No: there is no maximum, since $f'$ is never 0 at a maximum here.
options.why: You doubted the theorem. $f$ is continuous on $[0, 2]$, so a maximum exists: 2, at $x = 2$.

options.text: Yes, and the maximum is also $-2$ at $x = 0$.
options.why: You mixed up the values. $f(0) = 0$, and the largest value is $f(2) = 2$.

hints.text: List every candidate, not only the flat points.
The end points 0 and 2 are candidates.

feedback.correct: Right. The top is at an end, where $f'(2) = 9 \ne 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $f$ at the end points with $f$ at the flat point.

byKey.yes: You trusted $f' = 0$ alone. Interior extremes are flat (l18), but an extreme may sit at an end, where nothing forces $f' = 0$.

explain.text: Flat points are candidates only for interior extremes. The end points must be checked too: $f(2) = 2$ beats $f(1) = -2$. At $x = 2$ the slope is 9, far from flat.

screens.title: A stress test
screens.prose: A hedged book's P&L, in £1,000s, is $x^3 - 3x$ when spot moves by $x$ per cent. Risk asks for the worst loss over every move in $[-2, 2]$.
screens.question: What is the worst loss, in pounds?

hints.text: Check the end points $\pm 2$ and the flat points $\pm 1$.
The P&L is in £1,000s, so $-2$ means a loss of £2,000.

feedback.correct: Right. £2,000, at a 1% rise or a 2% fall.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest value of $x^3 - 3x$ on $[-2, 2]$, then convert from £1,000s.

byKey.units: You found the minimum, $-2$, but forgot the units: it is in £1,000s.
byKey.mid: You read the P&L at no move. The worst case is away from 0.

explain.text: The minimum $-2$ is attained at $x = 1$ and $x = -2$, so the worst loss is £2,000. It exists because the scenario set $[-2, 2]$ is closed and bounded. On an open set of scenarios the worst case may only be approached, as $x$ on $(0, 1)$ never reaches 0.

ideas: Extreme value theorem: a continuous $f$ on a closed bounded $[a, b]$ attains a maximum and a minimum. Drop closed, bounded or continuous and it can fail.
Bounded: if $|f(x_n)| > n$, Bolzano-Weierstrass gives $x_{n_k} \to c \in [a, b]$, and continuity makes $f(x_{n_k})$ converge, a contradiction.
Attained: pick $f(x_n) > M - \tfrac1n$, extract $x_{n_k} \to d$, and squeeze with continuity gives $f(d) = M$.

formula.name: Extreme value theorem
formula.tex: f \in C[a, b] \;\Rightarrow\; \exists\, c, d \in [a, b]:\ f(c) \le f(x) \le f(d)\ \ \forall x \in [a, b]
formula.note: Candidates: the end points and the interior points where $f' = 0$.

summary.trap: The maximum is not always where $f' = 0$: on $[0, 2]$, $x^3 - 3x$ peaks at the end point 2, where $f'(2) = 9$.

options.text: At every point of $[0, 1]$.
Nowhere: no value is larger than the others.
options.why: You read 'maximum' as strictly larger. A maximum only needs $f(x) \le f(d)$ for all $x$, and every point gives that.

options.text: At the end points only.
options.why: You looked for an end. Every point has value 5, so every point is a maximum.

options.text: At $x = \tfrac12$ only.
options.why: You picked one point. Every point attains the value 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the definition $f(x) \le f(d)$ for all $x$.

explain.text: For any $d$, $f(x) = 5 \le 5 = f(d)$, so every point attains the maximum. The same holds for the minimum. The theorem promises a top, not a unique one.

quiz.prose: Let $f(x) = x^2$ on the open interval $(-1, 1)$.
quiz.question: What can we say about its extremes?

options.text: The minimum 0 is attained at 0; the supremum 1 is not attained.
Both are attained, since $x^2$ is continuous.
options.why: You dropped closedness. $x^2 < 1$ for every $x$ in $(-1, 1)$, so 1 is never reached.

options.text: Neither is attained, since the interval is open.
options.why: You overcorrected. Open ends can lose a top; the bottom $f(0) = 0$ is still reached.

options.text: The maximum is 0, at the flat point $x = 0$.
options.why: You took the flat point for a maximum. At 0 the parabola has its minimum.

feedback.correct: Right. The theorem's failure costs the top here, not the bottom.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether $x^2$ reaches 0 and whether it reaches 1 on $(-1, 1)$.

explain.text: $f(0) = 0 \le x^2$, so the minimum is attained. The values approach 1 near $\pm 1$ but never equal it. Without a closed interval the theorem promises nothing, and here it loses the top.

quiz.question: Select all that apply: where is the minimum attained?

options.why: $f(-1) = 2$, the maximum.
$f(2) = 2$, the maximum.
$f(0) = 0$, neither extreme.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Evaluate $f$ at $-2$, $-1$, 1 and 2.

explain.text: $f(1) = 1 - 3 = -2$ and $f(-2) = -8 + 6 = -2$. Both give the minimum $-2$. One is a flat point inside and one is an end.

quiz.prose: $f$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$ and $f(x) > 0$ for every $x$.
quiz.question: Must there be $m > 0$ with $f(x) \ge m$ for every $x$?

options.text: Yes: the minimum is attained at some $c$, so take $m = f(c) > 0$.
No: the values could creep down towards 0.
options.why: You forgot the theorem. On a closed interval the infimum is a value $f(c)$, and $f(c) > 0$.

options.text: Only if $f$ is differentiable.
options.why: You added a hypothesis. Continuity on $[0, 1]$ is enough.

options.text: Yes, and the same holds on $(0, 1)$.
options.why: On $(0, 1)$, $f(x) = x$ is positive with infimum 0, so no $m > 0$ works.

feedback.correct: Right. An attained minimum is a positive value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the theorem to the minimum.

explain.text: By the theorem, $f(c) \le f(x)$ for some $c$ and all $x$. Since $f(c) > 0$, $m = f(c)$ works. On an open interval this fails: $x$ on $(0, 1)$.
